Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. source.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization aligns large language models (LLMs) with human preferences using only forward passes, keeping memory close to inference cost, but its gradient-estimation variance grows with the parameter dimension D. We propose deriving the ZO perturbation subspace from the preference data itself: a one-time, offline backpropagation over a small set of preference pairs yields per-pair gradients whose top principal directions span a k-dimensional subspace (k ≤128) in which on-device, forward-only optimization proceeds. We introduce the capture ratio ρ as a measurable quality index of a subspace, prove that the expected per-step progress of subspace ZO-SGD scales as ρ/(k+2) with a loss floor governed by 1 – ρ, and show that random subspaces (ρ ≈ k/D) provide no advantage over full-space ZO. A CountSketch–Gram estimator measures ρ at the 1.31 × 109-parameter scale without materializing the subspace. On Qwen2.5-1.5B aligned with direct preference optimization (DPO), preference subspaces attain ρ=4.6 10−2 at k =16—about 106times the random baseline—and, in×our setting, ρ is invariant when D shrinks by 127×, indicating that it tracks the effective rank of the preference-gradient distribution rather than D. Against six stronger low-dimensional alternatives—SFT-gradient spectra, magnitude/Fisher-style masks, structured low-rank random projections, and calibrated full-space ZO—only preference-gradient PCA both reaches high ρ and turns it into training descent, improving held-out DPO loss from 0.694 to 0.619; the alternatives stall or worsen. Peak training memory is 5.2–8.0 GB, versus 16.3 GB for a strictly matched QLoRA baseline.
